parts.html: Whether a kitchen is comfortable to use is decided at the layout stage: where the sink, stove, and refrigerator go and how many steps separate them. These are the rules we start a project with:
The layout is chosen to fit the shape and size of the room:

items: “Small kitchens”: A straight or L-shaped layout: the sink, stove, and refrigerator go along one or two walls, and the middle of the room stays free.
“Narrow kitchens”: The units run along the long wall, either in a single line or in an L. A U-shaped layout only works if there is at least 100–120 cm of clearance between the runs.
“Square kitchens”: A galley layout works well: the sink and stove in one run, the refrigerator, oven, and tall storage cabinets in the other.

parts.html: The work triangle is the three main zones of a kitchen: refrigerator, stove, and sink. How they are placed decides how easy it is to cook. As a guide, keep 1.2 to 2.7 m between any two of them: closer feels cramped, farther means extra steps. Here is how it plays out in different layouts:

items: “Straight layout”: Everything along one wall. It suits narrow kitchens, but on a long run you walk back and forth a lot between the refrigerator and the stove.
“L-shaped layout”: Works for most kitchens. The sink and stove usually go on either side of the corner and the refrigerator at the end of one run, so every zone is two or three steps away.
“U-shaped layout”: For spacious kitchens, with the most countertop and cabinet space. The downside is that three runs of units look heavy, so one side often goes without upper cabinets.

parts.html: An island or peninsula adds countertop and cabinet space but needs free room around it:

items: “Island”: You need a spacious kitchen, with at least 100 cm of clearance around the island. It can be a work surface, a breakfast spot, or the place for the cooktop and sink, in which case the plumbing and wiring are run to it during the renovation.
“Peninsula”: One side joins a wall or a run of units, so it takes up less space than an island. It often doubles as a breakfast bar and separates the kitchen from the living room.

parts.html: A few dimensions worth checking on the plan:

items: “Walkways”: Between runs of units, or between the countertop and the island, allow at least 100 cm if one person cooks and about 120 cm if two do.
“Windows and balcony”: If the countertop runs under a window, make sure the sash clears the faucet and the balcony door opens without hitting the cabinets.
“Cabinet height”: The countertop usually sits at 85–90 cm, and the bottom edge of the upper cabinets 50–60 cm above it. The exact figures are set to the height of whoever cooks most.

parts.html: Kitchen materials are chosen first for how they handle water, grease, and heat, and only then for color:

items: “Materials”: Stone (quartz composite, granite), ceramic, or stainless steel work well for countertops because water and hot pans don’t harm them. Wood is possible too, but it needs regular re-oiling, especially around the sink.
“Colors”: In a small kitchen, light fronts make the room look bigger. Dark ones suit a spacious kitchen, or just the lower run: with light uppers, the kitchen doesn’t feel heavy.

parts.html: Appliances and lighting go into the design before the renovation, because the outlets and connection points depend on them:

items: “Built-in appliances”: Choose the oven, dishwasher, and refrigerator models before ordering the kitchen: the cabinets are built with openings sized exactly for them and with dedicated outlets, and an induction cooktop needs its own electrical circuit.

“Lighting”: One ceiling light isn’t enough in a kitchen: at the countertop you stand with your back to the center of the room and block your own light. You need under-cabinet lighting over the work surface, a pendant over the dining table, and the general lighting on a separate switch.

parts.html: To give everything a place and keep it within easy reach:

items: “Ceiling-height cabinets”: Upper cabinets that go up to the ceiling, or in two tiers, add one or two more shelves for dishes you rarely use, and no dust collects on top.
“Drawers”: In the lower run, drawers are easier to use than hinged cabinets: a drawer pulls out all the way, so you don’t have to bend down and dig for a pot at the back.
“Organizers”: Cutlery trays, lid dividers, and pull-out mechanisms in corner cabinets give everything its own spot and put the corner to use.

parts.html: Details are usually what give a kitchen its character:

items: “Decorative elements”: A painting or poster on a blank wall, potted herbs on the windowsill, brass or leather handles instead of standard ones. Handles and decor are easy to swap later if you want to refresh the kitchen.
“Functional accents”: The faucet, the light over the table, an open shelf: things you use every day can also stand out. A black or brass faucet on a light countertop, for example.

parts.html: People also eat breakfast and sit with guests in the kitchen, so plan for that too:

items: “Upholstered seating and textiles”: If there is room, a corner bench or a banquette with drawers inside can go by the dining table. For kitchen curtains and seat covers, choose fabrics that are easy to wash.

“Range hood”: The hood should be at least as wide as the cooktop. A hood ducted to a ventilation shaft removes odors better than a recirculating model with a charcoal filter, so if there is a shaft nearby, go with a ducted one.

parts.html: An eco-friendly kitchen comes down to two choices: what the furniture is made of and how much electricity the appliances use:

items: “Eco-friendly materials”: For furniture and finishes, choose wood, veneer, laminated chipboard and MDF with low formaldehyde emissions, and water-based paints.
“Energy-efficient appliances”: Choose appliances with a high energy efficiency class to cut your electricity costs.
